briefOverview: Ezekiel condemns false prophets and prophetesses who speak from their own hearts, promising peace where there is none, and announces divine judgment on their deceptive practices.
summary: God charges Ezekiel to pronounce woe on Israel’s prophets who follow their own spirit and speak lies, comparing them to foxes and declaring that their visions and divinations are vanity. Because they have seduced the people by proclaiming peace when there is none, God pronounces that these prophets will be rejected—excluded from the assembly and the records of Israel—and that their protective wall, patched with untempered mortar, will be broken down. The prophet then denounces certain women who use ritualized items (pillows and kerchiefs) to 'hunt' souls and profit from misleading people, promising that God will tear these devices away and free the people. The chapter closes with the promise that such deceptive practices will cease and that the people will be delivered from the hands of these false seers so that they will know the LORD.
externalContext: Ezekiel was a prophet among the Judean exiles in Babylon after the first deportations (early sixth century BCE). His audience includes both fellow exiles and, by prophetic pronouncement, those in Judah and Jerusalem; this chapter reflects tensions about how prophets interpreted disaster and assured or misled people during the crisis surrounding Jerusalem’s downfall. False prophecy was a recurring concern in the Hebrew prophetic corpus and in the legal-prophetic traditions that warn against self-styled prophets whose messages contradict God’s word.
externalReferences: This condemnation of prophets who say 'The LORD says' when he has not spoken echoes Deuteronomy 18:20–22, which sets the criterion for identifying true and false prophets. Jeremiah addresses similar issues of deceitful prophecy and prophets promising peace where there is none (see Jeremiah 23:16–17, 23–32 and Jeremiah 14:14). The image of superficial healing and worthless assurances also recalls passages like Isaiah 30:10–11 and Jeremiah 6:14, where prophets and leaders give false comfort to a nation facing judgment.
practicalQuestions: How can communities today discern between authentic and misleading religious leadership?
What safeguards should be in place when hopeful messages contradict observable reality or ethical responsibility?
In what ways might well-intentioned comfort become a form of deception that prevents needed repentance or change?
How should victims of spiritual manipulation be supported and restored by their communities?
uncertainAreas: The precise cultural practices referred to by 'pillows' and 'kerchiefs' and the exact nature of the prophetesses' rituals are not fully explained in the text and may reflect specific folk or divinatory customs that are debated by scholars. It is also ambiguous whether all the condemned prophets were physically within the land or among exiles; Ezekiel’s audience and the identities of individual prophets are not specified.
